A precaution is an action you take before something bad happens, specifically to stop it from happening — or at least to reduce the harm if it does happen.

The key word is before. A precaution is never something you do after the problem has already arrived. It is always something done in advance, while things are still okay, because you are aware that something could go wrong.

Think of it this way: you don't put on a helmet after you fall off a bicycle. You put it on before you ride, because you know a fall is possible. That act of putting on the helmet beforehand — that is a precaution.

For something to be called a precaution, three things are usually present:

1. There is a risk. Something bad could happen — not necessarily that it will, just that it might. There is some level of danger, uncertainty, or possibility of harm.

2. You are aware of that risk. You have thought about it, even briefly. A precaution is a conscious, deliberate act — not an accident.

3. You act in advance to protect against it. You do something now, while the danger hasn't arrived yet, to prepare for or prevent it.

A precaution is therefore a form of intelligent, forward-thinking self-protection.

• You live in an area where earthquakes sometimes happen. You store some emergency water and food at home. That is a precaution.
  • You are going hiking and the sky looks a little cloudy. You bring a raincoat just in case. That is a precaution.
  • You are cooking with oil and you keep a fire extinguisher nearby. That is a precaution.
  • A doctor gives you a vaccine against a disease you don't have yet. That is a precaution.
  • You lock your car even when you park in a safe-looking area. That is a precaution.

In each case, the bad thing has not happened yet. But you are doing something now to make sure it either doesn't happen, or is less damaging if it does.
"As a Precaution" — A Very Common Phrase

You will very often see or hear the phrase "as a precaution." This phrase is used when someone takes a protective action even though the danger is not certain — just possible.

For example:

  • "The building was evacuated as a precaution after a small gas leak was detected nearby." — The building might not have been in danger, but people left anyway, just to be safe.
  • "Doctors kept the patient overnight as a precaution." — The patient was probably fine, but the doctors wanted to be sure.

This phrase carries a very important meaning: the action is being taken out of caution and care, not because disaster is guaranteed. It signals that someone is being responsible and careful.
"Take Precautions" — The Most Common Way to Use This Word

The most natural and common way to use this word is with the verb take. You take a precaution, or you take precautions (plural).

  • "You should take precautions before travelling to a country with extreme weather."
  • "She took every precaution to make sure the experiment was safe."
  • "The government urged citizens to take basic precautions during the outbreak."

You can also say someone failed to take precautions, which means they were careless and did not protect themselves or others when they should have.
The Difference Between Singular and Plural

You will see both "a precaution" (singular) and "precautions" (plural), and both are common.

  • The singular ("a precaution") usually refers to one specific protective action: "Wearing a seatbelt is a basic precaution."
  • The plural ("precautions") usually refers to a set of protective actions taken together: "The factory has put several safety precautions in place."

Both are correct and natural depending on context.

Understanding what a word does not mean is just as important as understanding what it does mean.

  • A precaution is not a cure or a solution. A cure fixes a problem after it has happened. A precaution tries to prevent it before it happens.
  • A precaution is not a guarantee. Taking a precaution does not mean the bad thing will definitely not happen. It means you are reducing the risk. A person can wear sunscreen every day (a precaution against skin damage) and still get sunburned on one very hot day.
  • A precaution is not just any preparation. You prepare for a birthday party, but you don't take "precautions" for it, because a birthday party is a happy event, not a risk. A precaution is specifically tied to the idea of danger or something going wrong.

Precautions can be small or large. They can be simple personal habits or massive organizational policies.

  • A small, personal precaution: washing your hands before eating.
  • A large-scale precaution: a government banning international flights to prevent the spread of a disease.

Some precautions are described as basic or simple — meaning anyone should be doing them without much effort. Others are described as extreme or drastic — meaning they go beyond the ordinary because the risk is very serious.

You might also hear extra precautions or added precautions, which means doing more than the usual amount of care because the situation is particularly sensitive or dangerous.

When someone uses the word "precaution," it generally carries a tone of responsibility and care. Taking precautions is seen as wise and mature behavior. Failing to take precautions is seen as reckless or negligent.

If someone says, "I took no precautions," it sounds like a confession of carelessness. If someone says, "I took every precaution possible," it signals that they were thorough and responsible.

A precaution is a deliberate action taken in advance to protect against a possible danger or harm. It reflects awareness of risk and a choice to act carefully before something goes wrong. It does not guarantee safety, but it reduces the chance or severity of harm. It is always tied to something negative or risky — never to a happy or neutral event. The most common expressions are take a precaution, take precautions, and as a precaution.
